big: Most people pick a fund by its return. A better first question is: how big a fall can this person sit through without selling? The fund must fit the answer.

lines: I'm nervous about equity. Where do I begin? I have ₹5 lakh.
First tell me this: if ₹5 lakh showed ₹4.4 lakh after a bad few months, would you stay put? Let us measure it, then match funds to it.

alt: Bars comparing the fall Meena can bear, twelve percent, with the made-up worst fall of three hybrid funds
caps: Meena can bear a fall of about 12%. On ₹5 lakh that is ₹60,000.
A conservative hybrid's worst fall in the made-up record is about 5%. It fits with room to spare.
A balanced advantage fund's worst fall is about 11%, or ₹55,000. It fits, just.
An aggressive hybrid's worst fall is about 22%, or ₹1.1 lakh. That is nearly twice her limit.

h: Start gently, add equity as she settles
alt: Three bars showing a hybrid fund being joined by an equity fund over five years
caps: Year 1: all in a hybrid that cushions the falls. She learns how it feels to see a dip.
Year 3: she has sat through a dip without selling, so a pure equity fund takes a 30% share.
Year 5: more equity, if she is still comfortable. Each step is a decision, not a hope. Shares are examples.
The review each year is where this is decided.

title: Sound and unsound rules
stops: Pick the hybrid whose worst fall fits her
alt: A shield with sound and unsound rules for matching hybrids to clients
caps: Fit the fall first. Then start gently and let the client add equity as comfort grows.
Several hybrids holding the same assets add cost and clutter, not safety.
Rebalance the whole portfolio once a year, not fund by fund.

q: Meena can bear about ₹60,000 of fall on ₹5 lakh, and wants as much equity growth as that limit allows. The worst falls in the record are about 5% for a conservative hybrid, 11% for a balanced advantage fund, 22% for an aggressive hybrid and 35% for an equity fund. Which fits?
opts: A conservative hybrid, with a worst fall of 5%, or ₹25,000
An aggressive hybrid, with a worst fall of 22%, or ₹1.1 lakh
A balanced advantage fund, worst fall 11%, or ₹55,000
An equity fund, since its high growth will make up for the fall
why: It fits comfortably, but it leaves growth unused. She asked for as much as her limit allows, which is a larger share.
A ₹1.1 lakh fall is nearly twice what she can bear, so she would likely sell at the bottom.
It uses most of her limit: ₹55,000 of fall against ₹60,000 she can bear, so it gives the most growth that fits.
A 35% fall means ₹1.75 lakh on paper. Growth that comes later does not help a person who sold in the dip.

q: Rohan has ₹8 lakh he needs in 10 months for a house deposit. He wants it to earn a little more than a savings account. Which fits best?
opts: An aggressive hybrid, since it earns the most of any hybrid
A balanced advantage fund, since it cuts equity when risk is high
A multi asset fund, since gold and debt protect equity falls
An arbitrage fund, since the money is needed within a year
why: In ten months a fall may not recover before the money is due, so a fund with 65% to 80% equity is risky here.
It lowers equity at high prices but can still fall by double digits. Ten months is too short to wait for recovery.
It spreads risk, but equity is still part of it. Falls can still occur and cannot be waited out in ten months.
With a deadline under a year, a hedged fund that barely moves with markets fits better than one that holds real equity.

q: A client holds three hybrids: two aggressive hybrids and one balanced advantage fund. All three hold many of the same large company shares. What should the adviser suggest?
opts: Keep all three, as each fund house runs its own style of investing
Check the overlap, then keep one or two and drop the duplicates
Add a fourth hybrid so that the overlap is spread more widely
Switch all three into one conservative hybrid, to remove all risk
why: Different houses can still hold the same shares. Three funds with the same holdings are one bet, paid for three times.
Funds that hold the same assets add cost and tracking effort but little extra spread of risk. Merging them keeps it simple.
A fourth hybrid adds another cost and more overlap. The question is whether each fund does something different.
A conservative hybrid still carries equity and debt risk, so risk is not removed. It also changes the plan's mix.

q: At the yearly review, Meena sees her aggressive hybrid's equity share has drifted from 72% to 68% inside the fund. She asks if she should sell units to restore it. What is the sound reply?
opts: Yes, rebalance each fund every year or its category changes
Yes, sell units whenever the share moves more than one point
No, never review a hybrid, as the manager does everything
The manager handles it. Check the whole portfolio's mix
why: A fund stays in its category while its share is within the allowed range, here 65% to 80%, and 68% is within it.
One point of drift is normal. Selling on that basis would cost tax and effort with no gain for the plan.
A yearly check of the whole portfolio is still needed. The manager does not know her goals or other holdings.
The fund's mix inside its range is the manager's job. Her review looks at the overall split across all funds.

pts: Match the fund's worst fall to the fall the client can bear, not to the return.
Start gently and add equity as comfort grows. Money needed within a year suits arbitrage.
Avoid stacking similar hybrids. Review once a year and rebalance the whole portfolio.
